plan.contextChunk: This figure is a two-part free-body construction, panels (a) and (b), each pairing a small pictorial sketch with an isolated force diagram at its left and a legend of symbol definitions at its right. Both sketches show the same tan incline sloping down to the left, a small salmon block labeled A resting on a larger block labeled B, and a cord running up the slope; a rounded outline circles block A in (a) and block B in (b). In (a), block A is reduced to a black dot on a dashed line standing for the incline surface, carrying four red vectors: N_BA perpendicular to and away from the surface, T up the slope, f_BA down the slope, and w_A vertically down. In (b), block B carries five: N_B perpendicular away from the incline, f_AB and f_B both up the slope, N_AB perpendicular and directed down into the incline, and w_B vertically down. The legends spell the symbols out, among them "N_BA = normal force exerted by B on A" and "f_B = friction force exerted by the incline plane on B". Stacking the two isolations invites comparison of the paired contact forces and the reversed friction directions. The construction demonstrates how to isolate stacked bodies touching two surfaces at once.

interactionPlan.concept: Isolating each body of a stacked pair on an incline yields two separate free-body diagrams whose contact forces form equal-and-opposite Newton third-law pairs, and whose friction arrows point to oppose the intended relative sliding rather than any fixed direction.

interactions.teaches: A free-body diagram contains only the forces acting on the one isolated object: clicking A brightens panel (a) and its four vectors while B's diagram fades, and clicking B does the reverse, making the isolation step explicit.

interactions.label: Highlight third-law pair
interactions.teaches: The matched contact forces (N_BA with N_AB, and f_BA with f_AB) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction but act on different bodies, which is exactly Newton's third law.

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency of A on B
interactions.teaches: Friction along each contact surface reverses when the intended relative motion reverses, so friction opposes relative sliding rather than pointing in any fixed left/right or up/down direction.

demo_steps.title: Isolate block A
demo_steps.narration: Click block A in the sketch: only the four forces acting on A (N_BA, T, f_BA, w_A) stay bright in panel (a), while block B's diagram fades. A free-body diagram lists forces on the isolated body only.

demo_steps.title: Isolate block B
demo_steps.narration: Click block B instead: panel (b) brightens with its five forces (N_B, f_AB, f_B, N_AB, w_B). Notice B feels the reaction forces N_AB and f_AB from A plus the incline's N_B and f_B.

demo_steps.title: See the third-law pairs
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the friction pair: f_BA on A and f_AB on B light up along the same contact line pointing in opposite directions. Switch to the normal pair to see N_BA and N_AB do the same — equal, opposite, on different bodies.

demo_steps.title: Flip the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Toggle the relative sliding tendency to 'A tends to slide down': every friction arrow (f_BA, f_AB, and f_B) flips along its surface, proving friction tracks the direction of relative motion, not a fixed orientation.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Contact forces between two touching bodies always appear as equal-and-opposite third-law pairs acting on different free-body diagrams, and each friction arrow points to oppose the relative sliding you assume — so isolating bodies and stating the motion tendency are the two decisions that fix every arrow.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked rows, panel (a) on top and (b) below. Each row has three zones: left = isolated free-body diagram (black dot on a dashed incline line with red labeled vectors radiating out), center = pictorial sketch (tan right-triangle incline sloping down-left, salmon block A on brown block B, black cord up the slope, rounded gray outline around the isolated block), right = text legend defining each symbol with vector arrows over the letters. Use a consistent red for all force vectors, salmon fill for A, tan/brown for B, light tan for the incline. Vector labels use bold italic letters with subscripts (N_BA, f_BA, w_A, T, etc.). When a body is isolated, dim the other panel's vectors and sketch outline to ~25% opacity. For the third-law highlight, draw a colored glow (e.g. blue for normal pair, orange for friction pair) on the two matched arrows across both panels simultaneously. For the sliding-tendency toggle, mirror the friction arrows (f_BA, f_AB, f_B) about their contact-surface normal so they visibly reverse along the slope.

authoredContext:
Two Blocks on an Inclined Plane Construct the free-body diagram for object A and object B in the figure. Assume that the rope pulls object A so that it slides upward, and that object B is sliding down the slope.

Solution We start by creating a diagram for the first object of interest. In the figure(a), object A is isolated (circled) and represented by a dot.

As noted in step 4 of the problem-solving strategy, we then construct the free-body diagram in the figure(b) using the same approach. Object B experiences two normal forces and two friction forces due to the presence of two contact surfaces. The interface with the inclined plane exerts external forces of NB and fB, and the interface with object B exerts the normal force NAB and friction fAB; NAB is directed away from object B, and fAB is opposing the tendency of the relative motion of object B with respect to object A.

(a) The free-body diagram for isolated object A. (b) The free-body diagram for isolated object B. Comparing the two drawings, we see that friction acts in the opposite direction in the two figures. Friction always acts opposite the direction of motion or intended motion. Because object A is moving to the right, friction by B must act to the left. Object B is moving to the left relative to B, so the friction by A on B is to the right. The friction force by object A on object B is the third law pair of the friction force by B on A, and therefore these two forces must be in opposite directions. Because object B is sliding down the incline, the friction force by the ramp must oppose it and act up the ramp.

Figure a shows two objects on an inclined plane, sloping down to the left. Object A is on top of object B. A free body diagram shows T pointing right and up, parallel to the plane, N subscript BA pointing left and up, perpendicular to the plane, f subscript BA pointing left and down, parallel to the plane and w subscript A pointing vertically down. W subscript A is weight of block A, T is tension, N subscript BA is normal force exerted by B on A, f subscript BA is friction force exerted by B on A. Figure b shows the objects on the slope in the same manner. A free body diagram has f subscript B and f subscript AB pointing right and up, parallel to the slope, N subscript B pointing left and up perpendicular to the slope, w subscript B pointing vertically down and N subscript AB pointing down and right, perpendicular to the slope. W subscript B is weight of block B, N subscript AB is normal force exerted by A on B, N subscript B is normal force exerted by the incline plane on B. f subscript AB is friction force exerted by A on B. f subscript B is friction force exerted by the incline plane on B.

We now include any force that acts on the body. Here, no applied force is present. The weight of the object acts as a force pointing vertically downward, and the presence of the cord indicates a force of tension pointing away from the object. Object A has one interface and hence experiences a normal force, directed away from the interface. The source of this force is object B, and this normal force is labeled accordingly. Since object B s sliding down and object A s sliding up with respect to the interface, so the friction fBA is directed downward parallel to the inclined plane.

interactions.teaches: A free-body diagram contains only the forces acting on the one isolated object: clicking A brightens panel (a) and its four vectors while B's diagram fades, and clicking B does the reverse, making the isolation step explicit.

interactions.label: Highlight third-law pair
interactions.teaches: The matched contact forces (N_BA with N_AB, and f_BA with f_AB) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction but act on different bodies, which is exactly Newton's third law.

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency of A on B
interactions.teaches: Friction along each contact surface reverses when the intended relative motion reverses, so friction opposes relative sliding rather than pointing in any fixed left/right or up/down direction.

demo_steps.title: Isolate block A
demo_steps.narration: Click block A in the sketch: only the four forces acting on A (N_BA, T, f_BA, w_A) stay bright in panel (a), while block B's diagram fades. A free-body diagram lists forces on the isolated body only.

demo_steps.title: Isolate block B
demo_steps.narration: Click block B instead: panel (b) brightens with its five forces (N_B, f_AB, f_B, N_AB, w_B). Notice B feels the reaction forces N_AB and f_AB from A plus the incline's N_B and f_B.

demo_steps.title: See the third-law pairs
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the friction pair: f_BA on A and f_AB on B light up along the same contact line pointing in opposite directions. Switch to the normal pair to see N_BA and N_AB do the same — equal, opposite, on different bodies.

demo_steps.title: Flip the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Toggle the relative sliding tendency to 'A tends to slide down': every friction arrow (f_BA, f_AB, and f_B) flips along its surface, proving friction tracks the direction of relative motion, not a fixed orientation.

plan.keyInsight: Contact forces between two touching bodies always appear as equal-and-opposite third-law pairs acting on different free-body diagrams, and each friction arrow points to oppose the relative sliding you assume — so isolating bodies and stating the motion tendency are the two decisions that fix every arrow.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked rows, panel (a) on top and (b) below. Each row has three zones: left = isolated free-body diagram (black dot on a dashed incline line with red labeled vectors radiating out), center = pictorial sketch (tan right-triangle incline sloping down-left, salmon block A on brown block B, black cord up the slope, rounded gray outline around the isolated block), right = text legend defining each symbol with vector arrows over the letters. Use a consistent red for all force vectors, salmon fill for A, tan/brown for B, light tan for the incline. Vector labels use bold italic letters with subscripts (N_BA, f_BA, w_A, T, etc.). When a body is isolated, dim the other panel's vectors and sketch outline to ~25% opacity. For the third-law highlight, draw a colored glow (e.g. blue for normal pair, orange for friction pair) on the two matched arrows across both panels simultaneously. For the sliding-tendency toggle, mirror the friction arrows (f_BA, f_AB, f_B) about their contact-surface normal so they visibly reverse along the slope.
